title: Lines, angles and triangles
what_is_tested: These questions use angle facts (straight lines, vertical angles, parallel lines cut by a transversal, the \(180^{\circ}\) triangle sum) and similar or congruent triangles to find a missing angle or length. Harder versions put expressions such as \((3x + 10)^{\circ}\) on the angles, hide similar triangles inside one figure, or ask about the areas of similar triangles.
how_to_spot: A figure with crossing or parallel lines, or with triangles that share an angle, and a question asking for \(x\), an angle measure or a side length. The words **parallel**, **similar**, **isosceles** or **bisects** are strong clues.
method: Mark every given angle and length on the figure (or on a quick sketch).

Find the fact that connects what you know to what you want: a straight line or a triangle (sum \(180^{\circ}\), on the reference sheet), vertical angles (equal), parallel lines (corresponding and alternate angles equal, same-side interior angles sum to \(180^{\circ}\)).
For lengths, look for similar triangles (two pairs of equal angles, often created by parallel lines) and write a proportion with matching sides in the same order.
Write one equation, solve it, and answer the exact quantity asked; an angle written as an expression needs \(x\) substituted back.
Check with the figure: an angle that looks obtuse must be more than \(90^{\circ}\), and the larger triangle must have the longer sides.
pitfalls: Setting two angles equal when they actually add to \(180^{\circ}\), or the reverse, at a pair of parallel lines (concept).
Matching the wrong sides in a proportion, such as using the piece \(DB\) instead of the whole side \(AB\) (wrong_quantity).
Reporting \(x\) when the question asks for the angle measure (stopped_early).
Multiplying an area by the length ratio \(k\) instead of \(k^{2}\) for similar triangles (concept).
Trusting how a figure marked not drawn to scale looks instead of the stated facts (misread_graph).
calculator: Rarely needed: most angle questions are short linear equations you can solve faster by hand. The Scientific tab can help with an awkward proportion or a square root.

cards.title: Foundations: angle facts
steps: Find the angle you need and the angles you know on the figure.
Name the fact that links them: straight line or triangle sum \(180^{\circ}\), vertical angles equal, or a parallel-line angle pair.
Write the equation (for example \(x + 70 = 180\)) and solve it.
Check against the picture: acute angles are less than \(90^{\circ}\), obtuse ones more.

worked_example.stem: In triangle \(ABC\), \(AB = AC\) and the measure of angle \(A\) is \(40^{\circ}\). What is the measure, in degrees, of angle \(B\)?
walkthrough: Sides \(AB\) and \(AC\) are equal, so the angles opposite them, \(C\) and \(B\), are equal. Call each one \(x\).
The angles of a triangle sum to \(180^{\circ}\) (reference sheet): \(40 + x + x = 180\).
Choice D, 140, stops at \(2x\), the sum of both base angles; the figure shows angle \(B\) is acute, so it cannot be \(140^{\circ}\). Choice A wrongly assumes all three angles are equal.
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
d=lambda a,b: sqrt((P[a][0]-P[b][0])**2+(P[a][1]-P[b][1])**2)
ang=lambda a,v,b: N(acos(((P[a][0]-P[v][0])*(P[b][0]-P[v][0])+(P[a][1]-P[v][1])*(P[b][1]-P[v][1]))/(d(a,v)*d(b,v)))*180/pi)
assert abs(d('A','B')-d('A','C'))<0.01 and abs(ang('B','A','C')-40)<0.1
x=symbols('x')
ans=solve(Eq(40+2*x,180),x)[0]
assert abs(ang('A','B','C')-ans)<0.1 and abs(ang('A','C','B')-ans)<0.1
assert value(choices[answer])==ans==70
assert all(value(choices[c])!=ans for c in choices if c!=answer)

cards.title: Medium: parallel lines and similar triangles
steps: Mark the parallel lines and the equal angles they create (alternate and corresponding), plus vertical angles where two lines cross.
If two triangles have two pairs of equal angles, they are similar; list the matching vertices in the same order.
Write a proportion of matching sides, or an equation for the angle expressions.
Solve, and check that the larger triangle gets the longer side.

worked_example.stem: In the figure, \(\overline{AE}\) and \(\overline{BD}\) intersect at point \(C\), and \(\overline{AB}\) is parallel to \(\overline{DE}\). If \(AC = 6\), \(CE = 9\), and \(AB = 8\), what is the length of \(\overline{DE}\)?
walkthrough: Angles \(ACB\) and \(ECD\) are vertical angles, so they are equal.
Because \(\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DE}\), the alternate interior angles \(BAC\) and \(DEC\) are equal. With two pairs of equal angles, triangle \(ABC\) is similar to triangle \(EDC\).
Match the sides in that order: \(\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{EC}{AC}\), so \(\frac{DE}{8} = \frac{9}{6}\).
\(DE = 8 \cdot \frac{3}{2} = 12\). Enter 12. Flipping the ratio gives \(8 \cdot \frac{6}{9} \approx 5.3\), but triangle \(EDC\) is the larger one, so its side must be longer than 8.

cards.title: Advanced: angle expressions and exterior angles
steps: Write each labeled angle as its expression and note how the angles are related.
Use the right fact: an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it; parallel-line pairs are equal or add to \(180^{\circ}\).
Substitute \(x\) back to get the angle the question asks for, and check that all the angles fit the figure.

worked_example.stem: In the figure, point \(D\) lies on the extension of \(\overline{BC}\). The measures of angle \(BAC\), angle \(ABC\), and exterior angle \(ACD\) are \((3x + 6)^{\circ}\), \((2x + 10)^{\circ}\), and \((7x - 4)^{\circ}\), respectively. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle \(ACB\)?
walkthrough: Angle \(ACD\) is an exterior angle of triangle \(ABC\), so it equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it: \(7x - 4 = (3x + 6) + (2x + 10)\).
The exterior angle is \(7(10) - 4 = 66^{\circ}\). Angles \(ACB\) and \(ACD\) form a straight line, so angle \(ACB = 180 - 66 = 114^{\circ}\), choice D.
Check: angle \(BAC = 36^{\circ}\), angle \(ABC = 30^{\circ}\), and \(36 + 30 + 114 = 180\). Choice C, 66, is the exterior angle, not angle \(ACB\), and choice A is \(x\) itself.
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
d=lambda a,b: sqrt((P[a][0]-P[b][0])**2+(P[a][1]-P[b][1])**2)
ang=lambda a,v,b: N(acos(((P[a][0]-P[v][0])*(P[b][0]-P[v][0])+(P[a][1]-P[v][1])*(P[b][1]-P[v][1]))/(d(a,v)*d(b,v)))*180/pi)
assert P['B'][1]==P['C'][1]==P['D'][1] and P['B'][0]<P['C'][0]<P['D'][0]
x=symbols('x')
xs=solve(Eq(7*x-4,(3*x+6)+(2*x+10)),x)[0]
ans=180-(7*xs-4)
assert abs(ang('B','A','C')-(3*xs+6))<0.1 and abs(ang('A','B','C')-(2*xs+10))<0.1
assert abs(ang('A','C','D')-(7*xs-4))<0.1 and abs(ang('A','C','B')-ans)<0.1
assert value(choices[answer])==ans==114
assert all(value(choices[c])!=ans for c in choices if c!=answer)

cards.title: Challenge: similar triangles inside one figure
steps: Look for smaller triangles inside the figure that share an angle with the big one (made by an altitude, a parallel segment or a bisector).
Prove the similarity with two pairs of equal angles and write the vertices in matching order.
Set up a proportion (or an area ratio of \(k^{2}\)) with the parts the question gives you.
Solve, then check the answer in a second way, such as the Pythagorean theorem or the other triangle.

worked_example.stem: In the figure, angle \(ACB\) is a right angle and \(\overline{CD}\) is perpendicular to \(\overline{AB}\). If \(AD = 4\) and \(DB = 9\), what is the length of \(\overline{CD}\)?
walkthrough: In right triangle \(ADC\), angle \(ACD = 90^{\circ} - A\). In the big triangle, angle \(B = 90^{\circ} - A\) too, so angle \(ACD\) equals angle \(B\). In the same way, angle \(BCD\) equals angle \(A\).
So triangle \(ADC\) is similar to triangle \(CDB\), with \(A\) matching \(C\), \(D\) matching \(D\), and \(C\) matching \(B\).
Matching legs give \(\frac{CD}{AD} = \frac{DB}{CD}\), so \(CD^{2} = AD \cdot DB = 4 \cdot 9 = 36\).
\(CD = 6\). Enter 6. A common slip is to average 4 and 9 to get 6.5; the length is \(\sqrt{36}\), not the average.
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
assert P['A'][1]==P['D'][1]==P['B'][1] and P['C'][0]==P['D'][0]
assert (P['A'][0]-P['C'][0])*(P['B'][0]-P['C'][0])+(P['A'][1]-P['C'][1])*(P['B'][1]-P['C'][1])==0
assert P['D'][0]-P['A'][0]==4 and P['B'][0]-P['D'][0]==9
h=symbols('h',positive=True)
hs=solve(Eq(h/4,9/h),h)
assert hs==[6] and P['C'][1]-P['D'][1]==6
assert Rational(spr_answers[0])==hs[0]
